### G6. The trust boundary diagram for an agentic system

```
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| BOUNDARY A: enterprise control plane (fully trusted)       |
|                                                            |
|  [Identity]  [Policy engine]  [Audit log]  [Secrets]       |
|       |             |              ^            |          |
|  +----v-------------v--------------|------------v-------+  |
|  | BOUNDARY B: orchestrator (trusted code you control)  |  |
|  |  system prompt | tool router | authz check | budgets |  |
|  +----|-----------------|--------------------|---------+  |
|       |                 |                    |            |
|  +----v-----+   +-------v---------+   +------v---------+  |
|  | MODEL    |   | TOOL LAYER      |   | RETRIEVAL      |  |
|  | semi-    |   | deterministic   |   | filters before |  |
|  | trusted  |   | enforcement     |   | similarity     |  |
|  +----------+   +-------|---------+   +------|---------+  |
+-------------------------|-------------------|-------------+
                          |                   |
       BOUNDARY C: untrusted (content and third parties)
                          |                   |
                 [web, email, files]    [vendor APIs]

  1 Nothing crossing C inward is an instruction. It is data.
  2 Authorization is decided in B, never in the model.
  3 Everything crossing B outward is logged to A.
  4 The model is inside the boundary and is not trusted to
    enforce it.
```

**What it shows.** Three boundaries and the four rules that follow from them.

**Three things to point at.** The model's position, inside the perimeter but not a security boundary. Boundary C, and the fact that retrieved content and tool results arrive from it. The audit arrow running back to A, which is what makes the boundary assertable rather than asserted.

**The failure it makes visible.** Authorization delegated to a probabilistic component, and instructions accepted from returned content. Both are invisible in an architecture diagram that has no boundaries drawn on it.

### G7. The AI gateway as a control point

```
 CALLERS            AI GATEWAY                    PROVIDERS
 +--------+   +---------------------------+   +--------------+
 | app A  |-->| 1 authn + tenant resolve  |-->| model, cloud |
 | app B  |   | 2 policy + classification |   +--------------+
 | agent  |   | 3 redaction inbound       |
 +--------+   | 4 routing + model pin     |   +--------------+
              | 5 quota / rate / budget   |-->| model, in    |
              | 6 cache lookup            |   | private net  |
              | 7 call + retry + failover |   +--------------+
              | 8 redaction out + filters |
              | 9 log / trace / attribute |   +--------------+
              +---------------------------+-->| self-hosted  |
                     |            |           +--------------+
                 +-------+   +---------+
                 | audit |   | metrics |
                 | store |   | + evals |
                 +-------+   +---------+

  Put a capability here when it must be UNIFORM across all
  applications to be assertable to an auditor. Leave it in
  the application otherwise.
  It does identity, policy, routing, limits, redaction and
  observability. It does not do prompts.
```

**What it shows.** The single point through which all model traffic passes, and the nine functions that cannot live in eleven applications consistently.

**Three things to point at.** Step 2, where classification selects the route before cost or latency is considered. Step 9, which is the evidence base and the cost attribution simultaneously. The three provider boxes, which is what routing by classification buys.

**The failure it makes visible.** Policy implemented eleven times inconsistently, keys that cannot be rotated without coordinated releases and cost that cannot be attributed retroactively. Also the gateway's own three failure modes: a single point of failure, a change bottleneck teams route around and a second place business logic lives.

### G8. The human-in-the-loop placements

```
                 model output       ACTION       consequence
                       |              |              |
  1 PRE-ACTION   [ human ]----------->|              |
    APPROVAL      blocks              |              |
                                      |              |
  2 POST-ACTION                       |-->[ human ]->|  undo
    REVIEW                            |    reviews   |  window
                                      |              |
  3 SAMPLED                           |--------->[ n% ]---->
    AUDIT                             |      detective only
                                      |              |
  4 ESCALATION   [ signal? ]--yes-->[ human ]        |
    ON UNCERTAINTY   |--no--------------------------->
                                      |              |
  5 EXCEPTION    [ rule flags ]-yes->[ human ]       |
    ONLY             |--no--------------------------->

  1, 4 and 5 are PREVENTIVE.
  2 is CORRECTIVE and needs a real undo window.
  3 is DETECTIVE and is not a safety control.

  Placement 4: route on STRUCTURAL signals (nothing above
  threshold, required field absent, value out of range,
  schema failure, two passes disagree, amount over limit).
  Never on the model's self-reported confidence.
```

**What it shows.** Five placements positioned against the action, with the control class of each.

**Three things to point at.** Where each sits relative to the action, because that is what determines whether it prevents anything. Row 3, which is a quality instrument and is routinely presented as a safety control. Row 4's signal list, because the wrong input there is the most common design error in the set.

**The failure it makes visible.** A sampled audit described as the control that makes an irreversible action safe, and post-action review applied to something that cannot actually be reversed, such as anything already sent to a client.

**What it shows.** Two instrument sets on two clocks, joined by a feedback edge, plus the exposure window that quality's measurement lag creates.

**Three things to point at.** The blocking edge from offline sets to promotion. The three fast proxies, which move in minutes and are the only warning available before quality is measurable. The feedback arrow that turns every incident into a permanent eval case, which is what makes the loop compound rather than repeat.

**The failure it makes visible.** Evaluation as a launch photograph. Also the high-confidence stratum being dropped to save review budget, which removes the only instrument pointed at the failure mode that matters most.

### G10. The governance moment

```
  EVERY ARCHITECTURAL DECISION HAS A TWIN
  ---------------------------------------------------------
  TECHNICAL DECISION            GOVERNANCE DECISION
  ---------------------------------------------------------
  which model, which version -> who approves a change to it,
                                and what evidence is produced
  what the agent may call    -> who grants the scope, who
                                recertifies it, on what cycle
  what is indexed            -> who may write to the corpus,
                                whose entitlements filter it
  where the human gate sits  -> what an objection does, and
                                who may overrule it
  what is logged             -> who may read it, how long it
                                is kept, and it is now
                                regulated data
  how it fails               -> who is told, on what clock,
                                and who decides notification
  ---------------------------------------------------------
       |                                       |
       +------------------+--------------------+
                          v
             MADE AT THE SAME MOMENT
             by the same person, in the same record

  Made later, the governance decision is made by whoever is
  present when the question arrives, which is usually the
  person with the least authority to answer it.
```

**What it shows.** Governance is not a review stage after design. Each technical decision carries a governance decision that is cheapest to make at the same moment.

**Three things to point at.** The pairing itself, which is the whole idea. The logging row, because every observability decision is simultaneously a compliance decision and creates regulated data. The bottom line, because deferred governance decisions are not deferred, they are delegated downward by accident.

**The failure it makes visible.** A design document with a separate governance annex, which is the physical form of a decision made twice by two people who never spoke.

### G11. The risk tiering funnel

```
 INPUTS (8)               SCORE          TIER       AUTHORITY
 ----------               -----          ----       ---------
 autonomy        \
 reversibility    \
 stakes            \
 affected pop      >-> weighted sum -> T4 crit -> board / exec
 data sensitivity /     0 to 32       T3 high -> committee
 external exposure/     then four     T2 mod  -> function head
 regulatory char /      overrides     T1 low  -> named owner
 novelty        /
                             ^
                             |
  OVERRIDE 1  any single dimension at 4 floors the tier at T3
  OVERRIDE 2  output affects legal rights, entitlements,
              employment, credit, health or liberty: floor T3
              and require human decision authority
  OVERRIDE 3  autonomy >= 3 AND reversibility <= 1: floor T4
  OVERRIDE 4  novelty = 4: one tier above computed for the
              first operating period, then re-score

  Bands before overrides: T1 0-8, T2 9-16, T3 17-24, T4 25-32
  Tier by what the system CAN DO without a human, not by
  what it is intended to do. Intent is not a control.
```

**What it shows.** Eight inputs producing a tier that determines how much of every other control applies.

**Three things to point at.** The overrides, which matter more than the arithmetic because a pure additive score lets eight moderate answers outvote one catastrophic one. The authority column, because go-live authority is the one decision right in the lifecycle matrix that moves with tier while every other row of that matrix stays fixed. That is a narrow claim about decision rights and not about the lifecycle: six other things do change per tier, from oversight placement to logging depth. The novelty dimension, which decays as operating evidence accumulates and is therefore a measure of absent evidence rather than a fudge.

**The failure it makes visible.** A tier that changes no design decision, which means the tiering did nothing. Also self-tiering, where the team scoring the system is the team whose delivery date depends on a low score.

### G12. The lineage chain from source document to cited sentence

```
  INGEST                TRANSFORM              RETRIEVE/ANSWER
  +----------+  fetch   +-------------+ chunk  +----------------+
  | source   |--------->| doc v3      |------->| chunk c81      |
  | DMS/1471 |  hash h9 | eff 2026-02 |  v.7   | offs 4120-4880 |
  +----------+          | juris US    | embed  | emb model m2   |
                        | class conf  |  m2    +----------------+
                        +-------------+                |
                                                       v
   run r55 : query q, filters {tenant, current}, top-k 8
             used c81, c14 ; REJECTED c92, c07
                        |
                        v
   answer a12 : sentence 3  <-- c81 (doc v3, offs 4120-4880)
                sentence 5  <-- c14
   reviewer u77 : edited sentence 5, reason "outdated rate"

  Sufficiency test: a competent reviewer with NO access to
  the current system state can reconstruct why the system
  said what it said.
  The retrieved set is PERSISTED, never recomputed. Re-running
  the query months later against a changed index reproduces a
  different answer, and presenting that as the explanation is
  misleading rather than merely useless.
```

**What it shows.** Three levels of lineage, and the third one, retrieval lineage, which must be designed in and cannot be added later.

**Three things to point at.** The rejected candidates, which show what was available and not chosen and are what distinguish a governed selection from a lucky one. The sentence-level attribution, because disputes are about a sentence and not about a session. The reviewer edit, which is the difference between an assisted decision and an automated one and is frequently the decisive question.

**The failure it makes visible.** Lineage retention set by the engineering horizon rather than the dispute horizon. Observability data kept for weeks is kept for the wrong purpose when contract disputes surface years later.

### G13. The three lines of defense applied to AI

```
 +------------+  +------------------+  +--------------------+
 | FIRST LINE |  | SECOND LINE      |  | THIRD LINE         |
 | owns and   |  | sets the         |  | independent        |
 | runs the   |  | standard and     |  | assurance          |
 | risk       |  | challenges       |  |                    |
 +------------+  +------------------+  +--------------------+
 business owner   risk, compliance,     internal audit
 architect        privacy, security     external assurance
 delivery team    governance committee
       |                  |                     |
   tiers itself      re-scores a sample     tests the whole
   builds controls   sets the standard      arrangement,
   produces          tests design           including whether
   evidence          effectiveness          line 2 challenged
       |                  |                     |
       +------------------+---------------------+
                          v
     WHERE IT BREAKS FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
     1 the first line is the only line that understands the
       system, so challenge becomes theater
     2 the second line cannot test what it cannot read;
       evidence must be emitted, not assembled on request
     3 the third line arrives after the design is frozen and
       finds design defects it can only report

     Fix: second-line calibration sampling, objective
     triggers that bypass scoring, and evidence generated
     by the system rather than by a person before an audit.
```

**What it shows.** The conventional control model and the three specific places it fails when the first line holds all the expertise.

**Three things to point at.** The calibration-sampling arrow from line two, which is the cheapest working mitigation because it makes optimism visible rather than punishing it. The evidence arrow, which must originate in the running system. Line three's position, arriving late, which is the argument for pulling assurance into the design review at tier 3 and above.

**The failure it makes visible.** Effective challenge that cannot happen because only the builder understands the build. It shows up as a second line that signs everything and an audit finding written a year later about a decision nobody can now reverse.

```

    v                                    queue
  ACTIVATED   %  who completed one real  no trigger in the
```

**What it shows.** Six stages, one metric each, one distinct failure each.

**Three things to point at.** The ratio rule: eighty percent provisioned against nine percent activated is a workflow-entry problem, and no amount of awareness work will move it. The dependent stage, which is the only honest predictor of survival. The advocate stage, whose absence means the program pushes forever.

**The failure it makes visible.** A healthy-looking usage number covering a system nobody would escalate about, which will be cut, and the cut will be justified using the same usage number.

**What it shows.** Capability sequence rather than a list of use cases, with each use case's prerequisites visible.

**Three things to point at.** The entitlement layer, which no single use case pays for and without which four are impossible. The regulated use case sitting last, because sequencing it early means either shipping without controls or a public failure on the most-watched item. The exit plan attached to the client-facing case rather than treated as an end-of-life activity.

**The failure it makes visible.** Which budget cut costs a quarter and which cut costs the program. A roadmap that shows only use cases cannot answer that question, so the committee cuts by cost and removes a foundation.

### G16. The incident containment ladder

```
  BLAST RADIUS ---------------------------------------->
  ------------------------------------------------------
  1 disable one tool           narrow        minutes
  2 tighten a guardrail        narrow-med    minutes
    or threshold               (accept more false refusals)
  3 route affected traffic     medium        minutes
    to a human                 (preserves the service)
  4 roll back the prompt       medium        minutes
  5 roll back the model        wide          minutes-hours
    or version
  6 KILL SWITCH                total         immediate
  ------------------------------------------------------
  Take the NARROWEST option that contains the harm.

  Every rung must be executable WITHOUT A DEPLOYMENT and
  must be rehearsed before launch, evidenced in the
  readiness gate under resilience.
  A kill switch that requires a release is not a kill
  switch. A rollback path nobody has exercised is a
  hypothesis.

  Before any rung: PRESERVE. Logs, retrieved sets, prompt
  version, model identifier, reviewer records. The instinct
  to disable and tidy destroys the only evidence.
```

**What it shows.** Six containment options ordered by blast radius, with the time each takes to have effect.

**Three things to point at.** Rung 3, which preserves the service while removing reliance on the system, and is the rung teams forget exists. The no-deployment requirement, which is a design constraint decided months before the incident. The preservation step above rung 1, because containment and evidence destruction are the same action if nobody says otherwise.

**The failure it makes visible.** A containment plan whose only rung is the kill switch, which means every quality problem becomes an outage, so the organization learns not to declare incidents.

```
 subset   endpoints in     and index, so   and index,   identity,
 of data  sandbox mode     scores compare  shadow and   trace ids and
 (or the  (mocked tools    across runs     canary, no   model id
```

**What it shows.** Five environments with the artificial-intelligence-specific requirement of each, and four gates that promote a candidate release tuple rather than a code build.

**Three things to point at.** The evaluation environment, which most organizations lack and which is routinely collapsed into staging. The contradiction that forces the separation: eval needs a frozen corpus for comparability, staging needs a live one for realism, and one environment cannot hold both. G3's paired metrics, because measuring harmful output without measuring false refusal optimizes toward a system that refuses everything.

**The failure it makes visible.** An aggregate pass concealing a segment regression, and a promotion decision made on a corpus that does not resemble production, which makes every retrieval number meaningless.

### G18. The decommissioning flow

```
  DECISION TO RETIRE
        |
        +---> [1] EVIDENCE PRESERVATION
        |         logs, evals, decision records, model ids,
        |         prompt versions, review records, lineage
        |         retention set by limitation period,
        |         regulatory obligation and contract, which
        |         is counsel's determination
        |         extracted to a format readable WITHOUT
        |         the system
        |
        +---> [2] RECORD CONTINUITY
        |         outputs that entered a business record stay
        |         interpretable, with the prompt, corpus and
        |         model context preserved AT CREATION
        |
        +---> [3] MANUAL CAPABILITY RESTORATION  (BLOCKS: must
        |         complete before the system stops carrying
        |         volume) does the manual path still exist, is
        |         anyone trained, what is the real capacity
        |
        +---> [4] DATA DISPOSITION
        |         corpora, indexes, embeddings, caches, eval
        |         sets, logs, adapted artifacts, memory
        |         (the same derived-artifact map erasure used)
        |
        +---> [5] DEPENDENCY UNWINDING  (BLOCKS: must complete
        |         before an end date is announced) instrument
        |         consumption BEFORE announcing the end date;
        |         do not discover consumers by asking
        |
        +---> [6] KNOWLEDGE CAPTURE
                  why built, what was learned, why ending
        |
        v
  IF REPLACEMENT: both systems exist at once
     behavioral difference BY SEGMENT before cutover
     users' working methods invalidated -> adoption event
     evidence continuity across the boundary
     parallel running: cost AND end date, both at the decision
```

**What it shows.** Six workstreams, two of which can block the others, plus the four recurring migration problems.

**Three things to point at.** Workstreams 3 and 5 as the blockers, per 10.6: manual capability restoration has to complete before the system stops carrying volume, and dependency unwinding before an end date is announced, so either one moves the date rather than the plan. Workstream 1 is not a blocker in that sense but is the one that most often adds quarters, because a retention period set by counsel can outlive the system by years. The derived-artifact map appearing here for the second time, having first been built for erasure. Parallel running with a stated end date, because parallel running without one becomes permanent and the organization then operates two systems, two control sets and two evidence trails.

**The failure it makes visible.** Obligations that outlive the system being discovered by whoever is present at the end, who is never the person who created them. Drawing this at design time is the argument for funding the exit plan as a deliverable.

## Appendix H: Vocabulary

Two runs. The core terms first, in one alphabetical sequence. Then the enterprise vocabulary, grouped by domain.

### Core terms

**5xx errors.** The HTTP status class (500 to 599) for a server-side failure to fulfil an otherwise valid request. **500** internal error, **503** service unavailable, **529** overloaded. Usually transient and resolvable with backoff, and categorically distinct from the 4xx codes, which indicate a client-side problem and mostly must not be retried unchanged. The retry decision rule is in 3.8.

**A2A (Agent2Agent).** A protocol for one autonomous agent to delegate work to a peer it does not control. Originated by Google in 2025, now a Linux Foundation standard. Three concepts: agent cards for discovery, tasks with a lifecycle, messages and artifacts for payload. The horizontal counterpart to MCP's vertical connection.

**Accretion.** What you have instead of an architecture when you cannot name the architecture. No known failure modes, no cost model, no precedent to review against.

**Adaptive thinking.** Reasoning depth managed by the model rather than set by a token budget. The only mode available on Claude 4.7 and later, which is the same fact as the removal of `budget_tokens` seen from the other side.

**Agent.** A system where the model dynamically directs its own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how it accomplishes tasks. Anthropic's simplest formulation: a model autonomously using tools in a loop.

**Agent card.** In A2A, a machine-readable document an agent publishes describing its name, capabilities, supported input and output types and authentication requirements.

**Agent Team.** Multiple agents working as coordinated peers, each owning part of a larger goal. One of the seven primitives, job COORDINATE PEERS. Distinguished from a subagent by direction: peers coordinate across, a subagent receives a scoped sub-task from above.

**Agent-computer interface (ACI).** The tool surface an agent works through. Anthropic's argument: invest as much effort in it as you would in a human-computer interface.

**Agent-to-agent.** A connection mechanism where two autonomous systems delegate goals rather than calling each other's functions. See the A2A entry.

**Agentic system.** Anthropic's umbrella term covering both workflows and agents.

**AI Fluency competencies (the 4D framework).** Anthropic's published framework of four competencies for human-AI collaboration: **Delegation**, **Description**, **Discernment** and **Diligence**, applied across three modes, **Automation, Augmentation and Agency**. Do not equate the three modes with the workflow patterns.

**Alignment.** Whether a system does what was intended. Model-level alignment is the provider's work and is not a control you can rely on; system-level alignment is the architect's.

**API.** Application Programming Interface. The direct HTTP interface to the model: you authenticate, send messages with a model name and parameters and receive a response. Using the API means owning everything around it, the interface, the conversation history, the error handling and the logging. Maximum flexibility in exchange for maximum responsibility. The middle layer of the platform map, alongside the SDKs, MCP and the Agent SDK.

**Attention budget.** Anthropic's term for the finite capacity a model draws on when parsing context. Every token spends some of it.

**Augmented LLM.** The foundational building block: a model enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory. Anthropic's guidance is that for many applications, optimizing single augmented calls is enough.

**Behavior properties.** The four properties of how Claude behaves that tell you what Claude can be trusted with.

**BM25.** A classical lexical search method weighting rare words more heavily than common ones. Complements semantic search, which cannot match exact strings reliably.

**Build-time Interface.** The middle layer of the platform map: how an engineer programs against Claude, the layer your code is written to. The direct API, the SDKs, MCP, the Agent SDK.

**Cache breakpoint.** The marker separating the cacheable prefix from the varying remainder. Everything before it can be reused.

**Cache write / cache read.** The two billing lines of prompt caching. Writes cost 1.25x base input for a five-minute lifetime and 2x for one hour, paid once. Reads cost 0.1x. The ratio between them is where cost savings live.

**Capability bloat.** Holding more tools or permissions than the role requires. Degrades tool selection and widens attack surface. Anthropic's test: if a human engineer cannot say which tool applies, the model cannot either.

**Chain-of-thought.** Prompting the model to reason before answering.

**Chaining.** The sequential workflow sub-pattern: step 2 takes step 1's output as its input, working sequentially and linearly. Anthropic's published name for it is prompt chaining.

**Chunking.** Cutting documents into retrievable pieces. Three approaches: fixed-size, semantic and hierarchical.

**Claude Agent SDK.** A managed agent runtime distributed as `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` for TypeScript and `claude-agent-sdk` for Python. It exposes the same agent loop that powers Claude Code, iteration, tool execution, observation and termination, so an agent can be embedded inside a partner's own product rather than run in a terminal. **Distinct from the Anthropic SDK**, which is a convenience wrapper over the API and runs no loop. The two are routinely conflated because engineers say "SDK" for both.

**Claude Code.** An agentic coding tool that reads files, edits code, runs commands and executes multi-step engineering work under configurable permission boundaries. Distributed as a CLI, IDE plugins, a desktop application and a web product. An entry point in the platform map, built for engineers, and customizable through the shaping and governing layers in 2.8.

**Claude.ai.** The end-user chat product, reached through web, mobile and desktop. Users sign in, open conversations, attach files, share context through Projects and connect services through built-in connectors. No code is written. **An entry point for users rather than builders**, which is the fact that rules it out of most embedding decisions and most regulated reviews.

**Coding agent.** One of the five reference architectures: agentic exploration with deterministic edit, test and review steps. Two phases: agentic investigation of the codebase, then deterministic edits following parse, plan, propose, test, review.

**Collaborative work.** The third delegation outcome: Claude drafts and a person decides. Distinct from AI-appropriate work and from human-retained work.

**Compaction.** Summarizing a conversation nearing the context limit and reinitializing with the summary. Anthropic's first lever for long-horizon coherence.

**Compensating control.** A control that limits the impact of a failure rather than preventing it. Usually the wrong choice where prevention is available.

**Consent fatigue.** The collapse of oversight when a reviewer is asked to approve so many actions in sequence that they approve without reading. The within-case counterpart to rubber-stamping, which arises from queue pressure across cases. The design response is to move review to a higher-value checkpoint, typically plan-level approval, rather than to gate every step.

**Constitution.** The published written document Anthropic uses during training to shape Claude's values and behavior, used both to generate training examples and to rank candidate responses. States a priority order for conflicts: broadly safe, ethical, compliant with the provider's guidelines, genuinely helpful. ⚠ **The ordering is holistic rather than strict**, so it supports a claim about tendency across a population of requests and cannot be cited as a decision procedure. Version in force is perishable; confirm before relying on it.

**Context editing.** A platform feature that removes old tool-result blocks from conversation history without restarting the conversation.

**Context engineering.** Anthropic's term for the strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during inference. The successor discipline to prompt engineering.

**Context rot.** As context length rises, recall accuracy from that context decreases. Emerges across all models. A gradient, not a cliff.

**Contextual retrieval.** Prepending a short model-generated situating note to each chunk before embedding. Anthropic's measured reduction in top-20 retrieval failure: 35 percent alone, 49 percent with contextual BM25, 67 percent with reranking added.

**Control register.** The table mapping each compliance obligation to a technical control, a named accountable owner and an evidence artifact, so a regulated deployment is auditable as a register rather than asserted as a narrative. Developed as the evidence register in 4.9.

**Corpus.** The body of documents a retrieval system searches over. Loaded and indexed ahead of time, which is exactly why it serves stable reference material and not live state.

**Correlation identifier.** A single identifier tying every step of one logical request together across model calls, tools and agents. Without it, multi-step systems cannot be debugged.

**Cost per outcome.** Total cost divided by completed successful tasks, rather than by API calls. The number that matters.

**Data processing agreement (DPA).** The contract governing processing of personal data on a controller's behalf. Where it sits depends on the delivery route: on a direct API it is with the model provider, on a cloud route the terms are inherited from the cloud contract. The route therefore decides which counterparty a notification, or a regulator, lands on.

**Decision logging.** Capturing the inputs, retrieved context, model output and routing for a single decision, keyed so that decision can be replayed and explained afterward. The same instrumentation as production observability, pointed at a different question: not whether the system is healthy but why this specific decision happened. The retention period and the query path differ accordingly, and the log is itself in scope for the compliance register.


**Delegation map.** The artifact decomposition produces. One assignment per part of the request, each justified through Reversibility, Stakes and Accountability.

**Delegation mapping.** The method for deciding which steps Claude owns, which existing systems own and which a human owns, with justification and control for each.

**Delivery Route.** The bottom layer of the platform map: where API traffic terminates, determining whose infrastructure the request runs on. The five routes are Anthropic directly, Claude Platform on AWS, AWS Bedrock, GCP Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry. Claude Platform on AWS is materially different from Bedrock in billing, feature timing and cache isolation, which is why it is counted separately.


**Dense (embeddings).** Semantic indexing: matches semantic similarity, meaning, not words. Earns its place where queries are phrased differently from the source. Paired with sparse and hybrid.

**Deployment lifecycle.** The eight phases a deployment runs through, per 10.6: discovery, design, build, validate, handoff, monitor, iterate, retire. Discovery and tradeoff framing do the first two, the eval gate is validate, documentation is handoff, the feedback loop is monitor and iterate, and the decommissioning plan is retire. **Two of the eight are least often designed for, the handoff in the middle and the end**, which is why a definition stopping at iteration is the common error rather than a shorter description. Naming the phase a decision belongs to is what lets you judge whether one phase is ready to move to the next. **Do not confuse this with the eight decision-right stages of 4.7 and F14**, which cut the same life on a different axis: a phase here is where work happens, a stage there is where somebody signs.

**Detective control.** A control that reveals a problem after it occurs, such as logging. Contrast preventive.

**Deterministic rule.** A rule that produces the same output for the same input every time. The category of work that must not be folded into a model, because a rule the business is counting on has to be right every time and a probabilistic system is right most of the time. The gap between those two is where the misroutes live.

**Dynamic Workflow.** One of the seven primitives, job COMPOSE AT RUNTIME. A workflow whose steps are assembled while it runs rather than fixed in advance.

**Effort.** A parameter that trades intelligence for latency and cost within a single model. Anthropic: tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. Defaults to high on Opus 5 and Opus 4.8.

**Embedding.** A numeric representation of a text's meaning, used so that similar meanings can be found by similarity.


**Entry Point.** The top layer of the platform map: the surface through which a solution interacts with the platform, what a person or system directly interacts with, the wrapper deciding who can talk to Claude and how. Choosing it is the fourth of the four decisions in 2.1. Note that the MCP primitive's definition uses the same phrase in the opposite direction, meaning points of access into your systems that tools expose.

**Entry-point responsibility map.** A written record of which entry point owns which task and why, produced before integration begins on any deployment spanning more than one route. Prevents the characteristic multi-route failure, which is drift rather than error: a route chosen for one task quietly taking on a second because no boundary was recorded.

**Eval.** Short for evaluation. A structured test set that pairs inputs with expected outputs or quality criteria, runs them against the model and produces a score comparable across model versions, prompts and configurations. The instrument that decides whether a change is an improvement or a regression before it reaches production.


**Eval contract.** The set of behaviors a reference architecture is obliged to demonstrate. Each reference architecture carries its own eval contract. You need separate eval sets per architecture, not a single eval set for the composed system.

**Evaluator-optimizer.** A workflow where one call generates and another evaluates in a loop. Fit test: responses improve when a human articulates feedback, and the model can provide that feedback.

**Evidence artifact.** The concrete proof a security or legal reviewer accepts that a control is live: a signed agreement, a configuration screen, an authorization record, a returned log query. **A control named in a design document with no artifact is a claim rather than proof**, and is indistinguishable at audit from a control that is not running.


**Existing systems.** The second of the three delegation owners: anything the organization has already paid to make reliable, such as the order-status service, the policy engine, the rules table or the database of record.

**Experience word.** A stakeholder's summary of a desired outcome rather than a requirement: seamless, easy, fast, simple, intuitive, smooth. **A signal that more discovery is needed, never something to record.** Converted into constraints by asking what would break the experience, what the user must never notice, and what must still be true when something goes wrong.

**Exponential backoff.** Retrying a failed call after a delay that grows with each attempt, usually with jitter added so that a fleet of clients does not retry in unison. The correct response to a transient error and the wrong response to a validation or permission error, which will fail identically however long you wait.

**Extended thinking.** A per-request capability where the model works through a problem in a separate block of thinking tokens before committing to an answer. **Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens and add latency**, and where thinking is not engaged none are generated and none are billed. The API may return a summarized representation of the reasoning rather than the full trace; billing follows the tokens consumed, not the length of the visible summary. Control has moved from a configured token budget to effort-based adaptive thinking across model generations, so verify the mode the target model supports. The decision to enable it should follow a measured accuracy gap, never the assumption that it cannot hurt.

**Fail closed / fail open.** What a control does when it cannot function. Fail closed blocks; fail open permits. Safety-critical and irreversible actions fail closed.

**Fallback chain.** The ordered set of alternatives the system uses when the primary path returns nothing usable: a lower model tier, a cached response, a deterministic path, a degraded mode. **Belongs in the orchestration layer**, because only the orchestrator knows what an acceptable substitute for the task is. The control most often built and least often exercised, which is why fallback behavior belongs in the eval suite rather than in the design document alone.

**Fast mode.** A research-preview setting on Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 delivering up to 2.5x higher output speed at premium pricing.

**Few-shot prompting.** Teaching by worked examples. Anthropic's guidance: curate diverse canonical examples rather than stuffing edge cases.

**Fixed-size / Semantic / Hierarchical.** The three chunking approaches, chosen by the structure of the source material, not by a default size. Hierarchical is the widest: it preserves document structure **and** retrieves at the level that fits.

**Gate.** A programmatic check inserted between steps of a chained workflow to confirm the process is still on track. Anthropic's term.

**GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation).** The European Union's data protection regime. Two points an architect keeps straight: it does not require European residency as such, because cross-border transfers are lawful with a valid transfer mechanism, and where a residency requirement nonetheless exists it usually comes from a contract, a regulator or internal policy rather than from the regulation itself.

**Generator-verifier loop.** Producing an output and then checking it with a separate pass. A mitigation for next-token prediction's precision failures. The same shape as evaluator-optimizer.

**Ground truth from the environment.** The tool results, code output or observations an agent uses to assess its own progress. Without it an agent cannot catch its own errors.

**Hallucination rate.** The measured proportion of outputs asserting something the source material does not support. A rate over a named population measured by a named instrument, not an impression. Distinct from groundedness, which asks whether an assertion is traceable to a retrieved passage.

**Harmlessness screen.** A lightweight model, typically Haiku 4.5, pre-screening input before it reaches the main conversation, with structured outputs constraining the verdict to a parseable classification. Applies to tool output as well as user input.

**Hook.** Developer code that runs automatically at a defined lifecycle moment, able to inspect, transform or block. The deterministic counterpart to a prompt instruction.

**Human-in-the-loop checkpoint.** A gate that pauses execution for review, positioned by the risk and reversibility of the action about to be taken. Distinct from the state-persistence sense of the word, meaning to checkpoint progress so a failed run can resume.

**Hybrid.** Indexing that runs dense and sparse and combines the results. The common production case: it recovers the exact-match results dense retrieval misses.

**Indirect prompt injection.** Adversarial instructions embedded in third-party content Claude reads on a trusted user's behalf: an email body, a fetched page, OCR output, a tool result. Distinct threat model from a jailbreak, with distinct mitigations.

**Injection point (fairness).** A specific place where unequal outcomes can enter a system: the retrieval corpus, the prompt framing, the chosen few-shot examples, or the downstream routing of the output. Naming them is what converts fairness from a model attribute you assume into an architecture property you instrument.

**Input screening.** A check running before the model call that decides whether a request reaches the model at all. Model-based where intent is ambiguous and the patterns cannot be enumerated; deterministic where the rule is crisp, because a deterministic rule cannot be talked out of its decision.


**Judge model.** A model used to score or classify another model's output on a quality a deterministic rule cannot encode, such as toxicity, tone or policy compliance. Evadable by construction, which is why it is chained with deterministic checks rather than relied on alone, and itself a system requiring calibration before its verdicts are trusted.

**Judgment erosion.** The failure where a team ships output it no longer understands because the output reads well and passes its checks. Distinct from the review-volume problem and moving in the opposite direction: volume degrades review by giving reviewers too much to read, judgment erosion by giving them something correct-looking that nobody can explain. The control is the human-understanding dimension of the verification checklist.

**Just-in-time context.** Anthropic's term for loading data at runtime through lightweight references rather than pre-processing everything. The same idea is also called progressive discovery.


**Latency percentiles.** Response time reported as a distribution rather than an average. The median describes the typical request and conceals the tail; p95 describes the experience of the worst one request in twenty and is the figure a service level is written against. A design reviewed on its median has been reviewed on its best behavior.

**Least privilege.** Granting only the capability a role requires. It means **removing** what is not needed, not supervising it.

**Live state.** Data whose current value is owned by a system and changes independently of any index: order status, inventory count, price, calendar slot, account balance. The correct answer at 10:00 may be wrong by 10:05. **Live state requires a tool call against the system of record, never retrieval over a snapshot of it.** The single most useful term in the reference-architecture vocabulary, because naming it is how the characteristic failure of 2.5 gets caught in review.


**Lookback window.** The twenty-block limit on how far back prompt caching searches for a previously written cache entry. Exceeding it silently loses cache hits.

**Lost in the middle.** The tendency to process the beginning and end of long inputs more reliably than the middle.

**MCP (Model Context Protocol).** A standard for exposing tools, readable resources and prepared prompts to any client that speaks it, so the service owner maintains one integration for everyone. Does not replace tool use; redistributes who maintains it.

**MCP resource.** Read-only data a server exposes, fetched proactively by the application without a model decision. Contrast a tool, used reactively when the model decides it needs something done.

**Minimum detectable effect.** The smallest improvement that would actually change the decision, fixed before an experiment rather than discovered from its result. One of the three inputs to a sample-size calculation, with the baseline rate and the variability of the measure. Naming it is what converts "did it get better" into a question a sample size can answer.

**Monolithic context.** Pre-processing and loading everything up front. Simple, predictable, cacheable, wasteful at scale.

**Multi-turn evaluation.** Scoring a system across a conversation rather than on one prompt and response. Distinct from multi-step evaluation, which scores one task executed across several internal steps. Checks three things a single-turn set cannot see: whether prior context is kept straight, whether a follow-up is answered without inventing detail never stated, and whether quality holds as the conversation lengthens. Requires its own golden dataset of full transcripts, which cannot be assembled by concatenating single-turn cases.

**Orchestrator.** One of the two roles in a multi-agent system. It owns the goal: it decomposes the work, decides what to delegate and synthesizes the results into a single answer. The orchestrator never does the sub-task work itself. Its failures are often unrecoverable, unlike a subagent's.

**Orchestrator-workers.** A workflow where a central model dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates to workers and synthesizes. Distinguished from parallelization by whether the subtasks are pre-defined.

**Outcome document.** The post-deployment artifact written for the sponsor who was not on the build and has to justify the deployment upward. Six fields: use case with scope boundary, metric before, metric after on the same definition, the control that makes the comparison auditable, the measurement owner, and reuse potential. Distinct from the value statement of 8.7, which argues the system is worth building; this establishes what it turned out to be worth.

**Output screening.** A check running before the response reaches the user. A judge model where the quality needs language understanding; a validator where the check is a known string, a forbidden field or a schema violation. **Judges text, not actions**, which is why it cannot substitute for authorization on a side-effecting tool call.


**Parallelization.** Running subtasks simultaneously and aggregating. Two variations: sectioning, being independent subtasks and voting, being the same task run repeatedly.

**Parametric knowledge.** What the model learned during training and carries in its weights. The model answering from memory, with no outside lookup. The opposite is knowledge supplied at request time: a document handed over, a retrieved chunk, a search result, a tool response. Almost every grounding decision in this primer is a decision to replace parametric knowledge with supplied knowledge.

**Per-turn budget.** One of the four constraints that bind an agent in production, alongside constrained tool entry points, explicit permissions and stopping criteria. Bounds consumption per step and is the runaway-loop control.

**PHI (protected health information).** Individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by a covered entity or business associate under HIPAA. Any third party processing it requires a business associate agreement, and **coverage is configuration-specific**: the same surface may be covered on one delivery route and not on another, so the check is by configuration rather than by product.

**Plan-level approval.** A pre-action human placement where the reviewer approves an agent's intended trajectory before execution rather than each step within it. The response to consent fatigue on long agentic runs. Composes with, and does not replace, a gate on any individual irreversible or high-stakes action inside the approved plan.

**Plugin.** A versioned bundle shipping skills, subagents, commands, hooks and server definitions as one installable unit. **Not** one of the seven primitives.

**Poka-yoke.** Designing an interface so a mistake is impossible. A manufacturing term, which Anthropic applies to tool design; their example is requiring absolute file paths so an agent cannot break by changing directory.

**Primitive.** A platform building block that combines with others. There are seven, each with a stated job: Tools (ACT), MCP (CONNECT), Subagents (ISOLATE / PARALLELIZE), Hooks (GUARANTEE), Skills (PACKAGE A PROCEDURE), Agent Teams (COORDINATE PEERS), Dynamic Workflows (COMPOSE AT RUNTIME). Slash commands and plugins are not among them.

**Programmatic tool calling.** Collapsing a chain of tool calls into a single script Claude writes and a sandbox runs, so intermediate results never enter conversation history.

**Progressive context.** Loading context in stages as the work requires it rather than all at once. Gives the model only what the next step needs, which keeps the working set focused and the per-call cost lower. **The right default for most production workloads.** Where it breaks down: tasks needing long-range coherence across the full history, decisions depending on detail dropped in an earlier turn, and caching, since a prefix that mutates each turn does not cache. It also complicates debugging, because the exact input the model saw at step N is no longer reconstructable.

**Progressive disclosure.** Revealing information incrementally as it becomes relevant rather than all at once. Appears at five layers: tool search, Skills, resources, retrieval and subagents.

**Project Skill.** A Skill held as a filesystem artifact in a repository, so it versions with that repository and is scoped to the projects carrying it. One of four Skill distribution channels, and the one whose rollback is simply a revert.

**Prompt caching.** Reusing the processing of a stable prefix across requests, cutting time-to-first-token and cost. Positional, exact-match, size-limited, time-limited.

**Prompt chaining.** Decomposing a task into a fixed sequence, each call processing the previous output. Trades latency for accuracy.

**Prompt injection.** Content the system reads, rather than the user types, changing its behavior. Controlled by treating all fetched content as data and gating actions behind checks content cannot influence.

**RAG (retrieval-augmented generation).** A pattern where a corpus is chunked and indexed ahead of time, and at query time the chunks most relevant to the input are retrieved into the model's context. Suited to stable reference material: manuals, internal documentation, policy and regulatory text. **Not suited to live transactional state**, where the index returns a snapshot that may already be stale and a tool call to the system of record is the correct mechanism. Retrieval quality is itself a system to evaluate and maintain, not a property that holds once configured.


**Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF).** The default for merging the two ranked lists a hybrid index returns: each result is scored by its rank in each list, and the combined score favors items that rank well in both. The standard, low-tuning way to do it. Rank-based scoring rewards agreement between the two methods.

**Reference architecture.** A documented pattern for how to wire an LLM application together to solve a recurring class of problem, already proven in the Claude ecosystem. References, not templates to adhere to. Five are named.

**Refusal (stop reason).** The typed signal returned when a provider-side classifier intervenes: on the Messages API, `stop_reason: "refusal"` with a `stop_details` object carrying a policy category and explanation. ⚠ Both fields are null where the refusal maps to no named category, and the object is absent on models predating the feature, so a handler must tolerate both. The category set is documented and perishable; read it at runtime rather than hardcoding it. **Reset the conversation context after a refusal**, since continuing on the refused context returns further refusals.

**Regular expression (regex).** A pattern language for matching text. In this material it appears as an instrument of code-based grading and of guardrails: fast, deterministic, free at the point of use and blind to meaning, which is precisely the division of labor with a model grader.

**Reranking.** A second, deeper relevance ordering applied to a retrieval shortlist.

**Residency pinning.** Constraining where inference executes to an approved region. Achieved through a delivery route or a request parameter depending on the platform, and not free: on some configurations it carries a multiplier on every token category, including cached reads, which is where a caching-heavy design concentrates its volume.

**Retrieval.** Fetching relevant material from an outside source at request time and handing it to the model with the question, so the answer is grounded in that source rather than in what the model recalls. Augments the context window; it does not replace it. **The model only sees what the retriever surfaces**, which makes recall failure a silent failure.

**Reversal cost.** What it costs to undo a decision after the system has been built around it. The third element of a tradeoff presentation, alongside what the choice gains and what it gives up, and the element most often omitted. **Distinct from the reversibility classification**, which sets how much process a decision deserves: a decision can be formally reversible and still expensive to reverse.

**Right altitude.** Anthropic's term for the correct specificity of a system prompt: between brittle hardcoded logic and vague guidance that assumes shared context.

**Routing.** Classifying an input and directing it to a specialized follow-up. Anthropic's named mechanism for mixed-model cost optimization.

**SDK.** Software Development Kit. A language-native library wrapping the API in idiomatic code, handling authentication, request formatting, retries, streaming and tool-use plumbing. **The same entry point as the API from the model's perspective, with different ergonomics**, and the default for most teams. The only reason to drop back to raw HTTP is an API feature the SDK has not yet exposed. Not to be confused with the Claude Agent SDK, which runs an agent loop.


**Sectioning.** The parallelization variant where a task is split into independent subtasks.

**Shippable.** Ready for production rather than working in a demo. Meets the accuracy, latency, cost and reliability bar the deployment actually requires, and has passed the evals and review gates the team uses to release. The distinction that matters: a prototype handling the happy path is not a system handling the long tail.

**Single sign-on (SSO).** Centralized authentication across an organization's systems. The architectural question it raises for a model integration is where the identity boundary sits relative to the model call: identity resolved server side and injected is a control, identity asserted in the user message is a claim the caller can edit.


**Sizing.** Capacity and cost modeling: volume, peak, token split, call multiplier, cost per outcome, sensitivity, feasibility.

**Skill.** A packaged reusable methodology defined by a `SKILL.md` file, loaded on demand. Shapes behavior within the existing capability set; does not create new capability.

**Skill distribution channel.** How a Skill reaches people, a decision separate from what kind of asset it is. Four channels, distinguished less by who receives the Skill than by what can be undone afterward: organization-provisioned, reaching everyone with no version pinning or native rollback; a plugin assigned to a group, carrying targeting, install preferences and version-controlled updates; a project Skill, versioning with its repository; and an API Skill, supporting explicit version pinning.

**Sparse (keyword, e.g. BM25).** Lexical indexing: matches exact terms, identifiers, codes, names. Earns its place on queries that hinge on specific tokens: part numbers, statute citations, error codes.

**Spend posture.** The administrative settings that bound consumption, decided at team setup rather than at operational review: the model default a session starts on, the allowlist of tiers the team may switch to, effort guidance, and spend, rate and per-user caps. **Inheriting the defaults is a decision taken by omission**, and at team scale it multiplies across every member and every request.

**Statement of the problem, as said.** The first column of a translation table, holding the stakeholder's own words in quotation marks. Not a stylistic choice: it is what lets a later reader check the translation rather than inherit it, since a row recording only the constraint has already merged the stakeholder's words with the architect's interpretation.


**Stratified sampling.** Sampling in a way that guarantees representation of rare categories, so a failure confined to one segment is still visible.

**Structured fields.** Named, typed values extracted from unstructured input, as against free prose. The unit of measurement for extraction accuracy, and the reason extraction is gradeable in code where summarization is not.


**Structured note-taking.** Anthropic's term for an agent writing notes persisted outside the context window and pulling them back later. Also called agentic memory.

**Structured outputs.** A platform feature constraining the shape of a response rather than requesting it. The deterministic answer to a format-compliance problem.

**Subagent.** A separate model instance with its own context window, instructions and restricted tools. A context-management primitive as much as a delegation primitive; **inherits nothing** from its parent.

**System of record.** The system that owns a piece of live state. The retrieval-versus-tool-call error is a system that searched a corpus of past snapshots rather than querying the system of record. Where a system of record exists, the answer comes from it, by tool call.

**The retrieval principle.** Retrieval is for stable knowledge: things that were true yesterday and will be true tomorrow. Tool use is for live state: things whose current value is owned by a system and changes independently of your index.

**Timeout.** The bound after which a call is abandoned rather than awaited. An unset timeout is not the absence of a policy, it is the policy of waiting indefinitely, and it converts a slow dependency into an outage of everything upstream of it.

**Tool.** A described capability the model can request. The description is the selection mechanism, which is why Anthropic says tool definitions deserve as much prompt engineering as the prompt.

**Tool-call authorization.** A check running before any action with a side effect, deciding whether this caller may perform this action in this context. **Deterministic by requirement rather than by preference**: an allowlist plus identity and scope, because an authorization decision has to be provable and replayable after the fact, and a probabilistic authorizer supplies neither property.

**Tool result clearing.** Removing raw tool outputs from history once they are no longer needed. Anthropic calls it one of the safest, lightest-touch forms of compaction.

**Tool search.** A server tool that keeps deferred tool definitions out of context until Claude searches for them. The answer to catalog scale, not to excess privilege. Anthropic names it an instance of just-in-time retrieval.

**Tool use.** The capability that lets the model call external functions, APIs or services during a response rather than only generating text. The model decides when to invoke, what arguments to pass and how to use the result. **The mechanism that makes an external system the source of truth**, and the correct answer wherever retrieval is being asked to own live state.

**Training-time alignment and inference-time control.** The two safety layers, distinguished by when they act and who owns them. Training-time alignment is the behavior baked into the model before any deployment exists, general by construction and owned by the provider. Inference-time control is the screening, authorization and review you add at request time to enforce rules specific to your deployment. **Conflating them leaves deployment-specific rules unenforced in every layer**, which is the characteristic silent failure of a safety design.

**Transient error.** A failure that will likely succeed on retry: rate limiting, an overloaded endpoint, a network interruption, a server-side error in the 500 range. The first of the four failure classes a resilient design distinguishes, and the only one retrying is the right answer to. Treating every failure as transient turns a permission problem into a retry storm.

**Translation table.** The output artifact of discovery. One row per item, four columns: the stakeholder statement as said, the implied constraint, the required architectural decision, and the assumption being documented until confirmed. The fourth column is the control, since **a requirement traces to something a stakeholder actually said and an assumption does not**.

**Verification checklist.** The explicit set of checks generated output must pass before production, written by the team for itself. Four dimensions: correctness, security, maintainability, and **human understanding**, meaning the person submitting the change can explain what it does and why. The first three are automatable and the fourth is not, because its subject is the reviewer rather than the artifact.

**Voting.** The parallelization variant where the same task is run multiple times for diverse outputs.

**Workflow.** A system where models and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. Your code controls the control flow.

**Working memory.** The third behavior property: whatever fits in the active context window. The window is a hard edge, not a gradient.

### Enterprise vocabulary, by domain

Grouped by domain. Where a term is commonly confused with another, the distinction is stated in the same line.

#### Enterprise architecture and operating model

**Application portfolio management.** The discipline of holding an inventory of every application with its owner, cost, lifecycle stage and business capability, and making invest, tolerate, migrate or eliminate decisions against it.

**Architecture review board.** The standing body that approves designs against standards and grants exceptions. Distinct from a governance committee, which decides risk acceptance; the board decides technical conformance.

**Business capability map.** A hierarchy of what an organization does, expressed independently of how it is organized or which systems it runs. The stable frame against which shifting systems and structures are compared.

**Center of excellence.** A central team that sets standards, holds scarce expertise and enables delivery teams. Fails in four recognizable ways: the **bottleneck**, where every team queues behind it; the **ivory tower**, where it publishes standards nobody consults; the **demo factory**, where it produces pilots and no production system; and the **tollbooth**, where it charges for permission rather than supplying capability. The tollbooth is the most damaging, because teams route around it and the result is a shadow estate the organization cannot see.

**Conway's law.** A system's structure mirrors the communication structure of the organization that built it. The practical consequence is that a boundary you want in the architecture needs a corresponding boundary in the org chart, or it will erode.

**Domain-driven design.** Modeling software around business domains with explicit bounded contexts and a shared language per context. Its value here is the bounded context, which is the natural unit for a corpus, a tool set and an owner.

**Federated operating model.** Central standards with local delivery. Contrast with centralized, where one team builds everything, and with fully devolved, where each function does as it wishes. The federated model is the common landing point and it fails when the standards have no teeth.

**Golden path.** The paved, supported and pre-approved way to build something, where choosing it removes work rather than adding it. A golden path that is slower than the unofficial route will not be used.

**Landing zone.** A pre-configured, pre-approved environment with identity, networking, logging and guardrails already in place, into which a workload can be deployed without renegotiating the controls.

**Operating model.** How work is organized, decided, funded and supported: the arrangement of people, decision rights, processes and platforms. Distinct from the organization chart, which shows reporting lines only.

**Platform team.** A team whose product is an internal capability used by delivery teams, measured on adoption and on the time it removes. Distinct from an embedded team, which sits inside a business function and delivers that function's outcomes.

**Target operating model.** The intended future arrangement of capability, process, decision rights, technology and people, with the transition path stated. Without the transition path it is a picture rather than a plan.

**Technical debt versus architectural debt.** Technical debt is local and repayable by a team in a sprint. Architectural debt is structural, crosses teams and is repaid only by a funded program. Reporting the second as the first is how it becomes permanent.

**Value stream.** The end-to-end sequence of activities delivering a result to a customer, cutting across functions. The unit that reveals queues between departments, which is where most cycle time lives.

#### Integration engineering

**Anti-corruption layer.** A translation boundary that keeps a legacy system's model from leaking into a new one. The correct place to normalize an enterprise resource planning system's identifiers before they reach a tool schema.

**API gateway versus AI gateway.** An API gateway does routing, authentication, rate limiting and protocol translation for services generally. An AI gateway adds model routing by classification, prompt and response logging, redaction, token budgets, cache orchestration and cost attribution. They can be the same product; they are not the same control set.

**Backpressure.** A downstream component signaling upstream to slow down rather than dropping work. The mechanism that turns an overload into degraded throughput instead of a cascade.

**Bulkhead.** Isolating resources so that exhaustion in one path cannot starve another. In practice, separate connection pools and separate queues per use case on a shared gateway.

**Choreography versus orchestration.** In choreography each service reacts to events with no central coordinator. In orchestration one component directs the sequence. Orchestration is easier to observe and to gate, which is why agentic systems that must be auditable are orchestrated.

**Circuit breaker.** A component that stops calling a failing dependency after a threshold and fails fast, then probes for recovery. Prevents a slow dependency from consuming every thread upstream.

**Confused deputy.** A privileged component tricked into using its authority on behalf of a less privileged caller. The canonical agentic form: an agent holding a broad service-account scope acting on instructions that arrived inside retrieved content.

**Contract test.** A test asserting that a provider still satisfies the expectations a specific consumer holds. Distinct from an integration test, which exercises the wiring; the contract test fails the provider's build, not the consumer's.

**Dead letter queue.** Where messages go after exhausting retries. A dead letter queue nobody monitors is a silent data loss channel with a reassuring name.

**Exactly-once versus at-least-once delivery.** At-least-once is what messaging systems actually provide and duplicates are normal. Exactly-once is achieved at the consumer through idempotency, not at the transport. Any design assuming the transport provides it is wrong.

**Idempotency key.** A caller-supplied identifier letting a server recognize a retry and return the original result rather than acting twice. The single control that makes retries safe on state-changing calls.

**N+1 problem.** Issuing one query for a list and then one per item. In agentic systems it appears as a tool that returns identifiers followed by a per-identifier lookup loop, which is a latency and cost defect the tool schema should have prevented by returning the batch.

**Outbox pattern.** Writing a message to a database table in the same transaction as the state change, with a separate process publishing it. Removes the dual-write failure where the state changed and the event did not.

**Poison message.** A message that fails every time it is processed and blocks the queue behind it. Handled by attempt counting and routing to a dead letter queue, not by retrying harder.

**Rate limit versus quota.** A rate limit bounds requests per unit of time and protects the service. A quota bounds consumption over a period and protects the budget. They are enforced in different places and breaching them means different things.

**Saga.** A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions for rollback, used where a distributed transaction is impossible. The compensating action is the design work; most sagas fail because someone assumed a step was reversible.

**Schema registry.** A governed store of message and payload schemas with compatibility rules, so that a producer cannot ship a breaking change unnoticed. The enterprise control that makes additive-only evolution enforceable rather than aspirational.

**Strangler fig.** Replacing a legacy system incrementally by routing slices of traffic to the new implementation until nothing reaches the old one. The realistic migration pattern where a big-bang cutover is unacceptable.

**Webhook signature verification.** Validating that an inbound callback genuinely came from the claimed sender, using a shared secret over the raw body. Omitting it turns a webhook endpoint into an unauthenticated write path.

#### Data and knowledge architecture

**Authoritative source.** The one artifact designated as correct for a knowledge domain, with every other artifact in that domain labeled derived or copy. Related to but not identical with system of record: a system of record is a system, an authoritative source may be a document, and a domain with two authoritative sources is not ready for retrieval.

**Conceptual, logical and physical model.** Three levels of data modeling: what the business means, how it is structured independently of technology and how it is implemented. An artificial intelligence system needs all three, because retrieval filters are written against the logical level and business meaning is what the model must reproduce.

**Controlled vocabulary.** A fixed list of permitted terms for a field, with synonyms mapped to preferred terms. Makes filtering reliable and makes an enumeration meaningful rather than decorative.

**Data contract.** An agreement between a data producer and its consumers covering schema, semantics, freshness, quality thresholds and change notice. Turns an implicit dependency into an obligation someone owns.

**Data lake, warehouse and lakehouse.** A lake stores raw files with schema applied on read. A warehouse stores modeled, curated tables with schema applied on write. A lakehouse combines file storage with table semantics and transactions. The distinction matters here because retrieval evaluation needs reproducible snapshots, which the lake does not give for free.

**Data mesh.** An operating model treating data as a product owned by the domain that produces it, with central standards and self-serve infrastructure. Its relevance is ownership: it names the person accountable for a corpus.

**Data product.** A curated, documented, versioned and owned data asset with stated quality and freshness commitments and a consumer-facing interface. A corpus intended for retrieval should be built as one.

**Data steward versus data owner.** The owner is accountable for the data and can authorize its use. The steward operates it day to day, maintains quality and definitions and has no authority to permit a new purpose. Confusing the two produces approvals from people who cannot give them.

**Derived artifact.** Anything computed from a source record: chunks, embeddings, index entries, caches, assembled-context logs, evaluation sets, analytics extracts and memory stores. The set an erasure request must reach and the set a decommissioning must dispose of.

**Document engineering.** Deliberately structuring documents so that a machine can use them: stable headings, one idea per section, tables as tables, explicit effective dates, explicit supersession and no meaning carried by layout alone.

**Entity resolution.** Determining that two records refer to the same real-world thing. The step where identifier mismatch across systems becomes visible, and the step where an agent must ask rather than guess when multiple candidates match.

**Freshness requirement.** The maximum acceptable lag between a change at source and its appearance in the retrievable set, stated in time rather than in effort. Drives the reindexing strategy and belongs in the user interface as a published commitment.

**Golden record.** The single reconciled version of an entity assembled from multiple sources by master data management. The thing an agent should resolve against rather than any one contributing system.

**Information lifecycle management.** Governing data from creation through active use, archive and destruction, with the basis for each transition recorded. The frame that turns retention from a storage setting into a control.

**Knowledge estate.** Everything an organization knows, across systems nobody inventoried, in states nobody recorded, owned by people who have mostly left. The thing retrieval reads from, whose every property becomes a property of the answer.

**Master data management.** The discipline of maintaining a single authoritative version of core entities such as customer, supplier, product and employee across systems. Its absence is why identifier resolution is the quiet cost in most integrations.

**Metadata, five categories.** Technical describes structure and format. Business describes meaning and ownership. Operational describes runtime facts such as ingestion time and record counts. Provenance describes origin and transformation. Governance describes classification, retention and access. Retrieval systems fail on the last three most often.

**Ontology versus taxonomy.** A taxonomy is a hierarchy of categories. An ontology adds typed relationships between entities, so it can express that a policy supersedes another policy or applies to a jurisdiction. Retrieval filters need a taxonomy; reasoning over relationships needs an ontology.

**Records schedule.** The formal statement of how long each class of record is kept, on what basis and how it is disposed of. The document that answers a retention question with authority rather than with a default.

**Semantic layer.** A governed mapping from physical tables to business concepts and metrics, so that "revenue" means one thing. The prerequisite for letting any system, human or otherwise, query the warehouse without inventing definitions.

**Supersession.** The explicit statement that one artifact replaces another from a given date. Must be machine-readable and must remove the superseded content from the retrievable set rather than merely marking it, or the model will cite both.

**Tacit versus embedded knowledge.** Tacit knowledge is in people's heads and requires elicitation before any pipeline can use it. Embedded knowledge is encoded in system behavior such as validation rules and workflow branches, is frequently the authoritative version and must be extracted into a tool call rather than described in a document. Only explicit knowledge is a retrieval problem.

#### Governance, risk management and compliance

**Assurance map.** A view of which risks are covered by which controls and which line of defense tests each, showing gaps and duplication. The artifact that reveals a risk everyone assumed someone else was testing.

**Attestation.** A formal statement by a named person that something is true as at a date, made on the record. Cheap, weak on its own and valuable because it creates an addressee.

**Control design versus operating effectiveness.** Design asks whether the control would address the risk if it operated. Operating effectiveness asks whether it operated as designed throughout a period. An organization can pass every design test and fail every operating test, and this is the normal first-year outcome for artificial intelligence controls.

**Control mapping.** Relating one control set to another framework's requirements so that one implementation satisfies several external expectations. Done once and maintained, it prevents the same control being built three times under three names.

**Control objective.** What a control is supposed to achieve, stated as an outcome rather than as an activity. "Only authorized users retrieve privileged material" is an objective; "run a quarterly access review" is an activity that may or may not achieve it.

**Effective challenge.** Substantive, independent questioning of a design or a result by someone competent to do so and empowered to make it stick. Breaks in artificial intelligence programs because the first line is often the only line that understands the system.

**Exception and waiver.** An approved, time-bounded departure from a standard, with a named approver, a stated compensating measure and an expiry. An exception with no expiry is a silent standard change.

**Inherent versus residual risk.** Inherent is the risk before controls. Residual is what remains after them. Residual risk is the number that gets accepted, and the acceptance names a person, not a committee.
